Project overview
About sRNA-TAPS
sRNA-TAPS is an open-source analysis pipeline developed in the Schneider Lab at the Institute of Chemical Epigenetics Munich (ICEM), LMU Munich. It adapts TET-assisted pyridine borane sequencing (TAPS) to study cytosine modifications in small RNA, where short, repetitive, and strand-specific molecules create distinct analytical challenges.
Built specifically for small-RNA data, the workflow combines TAPS-aware alignment, fractional handling of multi-mapping reads, biotype-resolved modification calling, and a three-condition framework for chemistry-based background correction. It supports analysis of m5C and hm5C across miRNA, tRNA, rRNA, snoRNA, snRNA, piRNA, and lncRNA with species-aware reference support, without the harsh degradation associated with bisulfite treatment.
Designed for
Small-RNA complexity
TAPS-aware alignment is adapted to short, repetitive, and strand-specific molecules.
Built around
Reliable signal correction
A three-condition framework supports chemistry-aware background correction from the start.
Covers

Modification calling is resolved across miRNA, tRNA, rRNA, snoRNA, snRNA, piRNA, and lncRNA.

Evidence
Benchmarking
sRNA-TAPS was compared against rastair, asTair, and Bismark to evaluate site-level concordance, modification rate correlation, and how well each approach handles small-RNA biology.
Bismark
rastair
Comparison scope
Three external callers
rastair, asTair, and Bismark are evaluated alongside sRNA-TAPS across multiple output and chemistry assumptions.
What matters
Biotypes and chemistry stay explicit
Coverage thresholds, multi-mapping behaviour, and TAPS-native signal direction are kept central to the interpretation.
Readout
Figures stay close to the claims
Concordance, shared-site correlation, overlap, and context behaviour are all shown directly below.
Framing
Why existing tools fall short for small RNA
Most methylation callers were designed for DNA or for long, abundant RNA species. Applying them to small RNA introduces three systematic problems:
rastair
DNA-oriented
Designed for TAPS data but optimised for DNA methylation calling. Lacks biotype-aware splitting and uses fixed coverage thresholds inappropriate for short RNA species.
asTair
RNA-compatible
Supports RNA TAPS but does not distinguish between RNA biotypes. Applies uniform calling parameters across miRNA, tRNA, and rRNA — which have fundamentally different coverage profiles and multi-mapping characteristics.
Bismark
Bisulfite
Built for bisulfite sequencing where unmodified C converts to T. The signal direction is inverted relative to TAPS — modified C stays as C in bisulfite but converts to T in TAPS. Bismark results must be inverted for comparison.
sRNA-TAPS addresses all three limitations —

Results
Benchmark results
sRNA-TAPS calls were compared against rastair, asTair, and Bismark across all RNA biotypes in HEK293 and Caco2 cell lines. Results show site-level concordance (Jaccard index), modification rate correlation at shared sites (Pearson r), and called site overlap.
Note on Bismark: Bismark uses bisulfite chemistry where the signal direction is inverted — unmodified C converts to T rather than modified C. Bismark mod_rates are therefore 1 − rate before comparison. Negative or near-zero Pearson r for Bismark is expected and confirms correct chemistry inversion.

Figure 4b — Pearson correlation at shared sites

Figure 4b — Modification rates at shared sites

Figure 4c — Called site overlap

Context
rastair in small RNA — a context mismatch
rastair was originally designed and validated for genome-wide DNA methylation calling, where CpG is the dominant and biologically most relevant methylation context. In that setting, CpG-only calling is entirely appropriate and the tool performs excellently.
However, when applied to small RNA — as we do here for benchmarking purposes — this design choice becomes a fundamental mismatch. The most biologically relevant m5C sites in small RNA occur predominantly in non-CpG contexts: C34 and C38 in tRNA wobble positions (CHH/CHG), internal positions in rRNA, and seed-region

chunks.title: Benchmarking — sRNA-TAPS
chunks.text:
al mismatch. The most biologically relevant m5C sites in small RNA occur predominantly in non-CpG contexts: C34 and C38 in tRNA wobble positions (CHH/CHG), internal positions in rRNA, and seed-region cytosines in miRNA are rarely CpG dinucleotides.
To confirm this, we ran rastair twice on the same BAMs — once with --cpgs-only and once without. The outputs were identical: the same sites, the same modification rates, the same Pearson correlation with sRNA-TAPS. This demonstrates that rastair's CpG restriction is implemented at the core calling level, not just as a post-processing filter, and cannot be bypassed via command-line flags.
This is not a criticism of rastair — it is working exactly as designed for its intended use case. It is rather a demonstration of why a dedicated small RNA pipeline is needed. sRNA-TAPS is currently the only pipeline that calls m5C in all cytosine contexts across all small RNA biotypes.
Figure 4d — rastair CpG-only vs all-context: identical output
Pearson r between sRNA-TAPS and rastair at shared sites, comparing the --cpgs-only run against the all-context run. The two lines are completely overlapping, confirming rastair produces identical output regardless of context flag.

Frequently asked questions
What sequencing depth do I need for reliable m5C detection?
↓
Minimum coverage thresholds vary by biotype: rRNA requires ≥10x, miRNA and snoRNA ≥5x, and tRNA ≥3x. In practice, deeper coverage improves sensitivity and reduces false positives. For miRNA, we recommend at least 20–30x coverage at expressed loci. Standard small RNA-seq libraries of 10–20 million reads per sample are generally sufficient.
Can I use sRNA-TAPS without a pb_Ctrl condition?
↓
The pipeline requires a pb_Ctrl condition for background correction. Without it, the delta (δ) score cannot be calculated, and genuine m5C signal cannot be distinguished from pyridine borane chemistry noise (~8–9% background C→T). We strongly recommend including at least two pb_Ctrl replicates per cell line in your experimental design.
Why are most of my reads assigned to the "other" biotype?
↓
The "other" category captures reads that do not overlap a uniquely annotated Ensembl feature, or that map to regions where multiple biotypes share equal priority in the annotation hierarchy. This is common in small RNA-seq data and does not indicate a pipeline problem.
Several factors can contribute to a high "other" fraction: reads mapping to unannotated intergenic regions, reads overlapping antisense transcripts or pseudogenes not classified under the main biotypes, and multi-mapping reads that cannot be confidently assigned to a single locus. In TAPS-treated samples, the chemical conversion step ca

anscripts or pseudogenes not classified under the main biotypes, and multi-mapping reads that cannot be confidently assigned to a single locus. In TAPS-treated samples, the chemical conversion step can also affect alignment scores at modified positions, occasionally pushing reads into ambiguous mapping territory.
To reduce the "other" fraction, ensure you are using a current Ensembl GTF for your selected species and release, that your alignment is to the full genome rather than a transcriptome, and that your GTF biotype priority list covers the RNA species most relevant to your experiment.
My alignment rate is very low — what should I check?
↓
First check that adapter trimming ran correctly — untrimmed reads align poorly. Verify that you are using --norc (forward strand only) and -v 2 in Bowtie1. If your alignment rate is below 60%, check the trimming report for adapter content and read length distribution. For synthetic test data, ~80% alignment is expected; for real data, 70–90% is typical depending on library quality.
Can I run sRNA-TAPS on mouse or other non-human genomes?
↓
Yes. sRNA-TAPS now supports species-aware reference setup, with built-in Ensembl-backed configurations for human, mouse, rat, zebrafish, fruit fly, c_elegans, and chicken, plus custom FASTA/GTF inputs for other organisms. For non-human runs, use the matching genome FASTA, annotation, and any species-appropriate variant resources you need for filtering.

How do I interpret a negative delta (δ) score?
↓
A negative δ means the pb_Ctrl mod_rate is higher than the treat mod_rate at that position. This typically indicates a SNP or sequence variant that causes elevated C→T in the background control, or a position where pyridine borane chemistry has unusual context-specific reactivity. Sites with δ < 0 are filtered out during the differential methylation step and should not be interpreted as biologically meaningful.
Why does the report show empty benchmarking figures?
↓
Benchmarking figures require the 09.compare/ directory to be populated, which in turn requires the benchmarking tools (rastair, asTair, Bismark) to have been run in step 08. If you ran the pipeline without the --benchmark flag, these steps are skipped. Re-run Snakemake with the all_benchmark target to include benchmarking — see the Tutorial for the full command.

↓
Please cite: Simsir Ö., Henzeler B. et al. sRNA-TAPS: TAPS-based m5C detection in small RNA. (in preparation, 2026). See the References page for a full list of tools and methods used in the pipeline that should also be cited.

Quick Start
sRNA-TAPS runs as a Snakemake 9 profile-based workflow. All SLURM resource allocation is handled by the profile — no cluster submission strings or job scripts to manage.
# 1. Create a project directory and add raw FASTQs
mkdir ~/my_project && cd ~/my_project
mkdir rawfiles
# copy *.fq.gz into rawfiles/
# 2. Create config.yaml and samples.tsv (see Configuration below)
# 3. Dry-run to verify the DAG
snakemake \
--snakefile /path/to/sRNA-TAPS/workflow/Snakefile \
--configfile config.yaml \
--profile /path/to/sRNA-TAPS/profile \
--dry-run
# 4. Run the full pipeline
bash /path/to/sRNA-TAPS/sRNA_taps.bash
# — or directly in the background —
snakemake \
--snakefile /path/to/sRNA-TAPS/workflow/Snakefile \
--configfile config.yaml \
--profile /path/to/sRNA-TAPS/profile &
# 5. Run with benchmarking (optional)
snakemake \
--snakefile /path/to/sRNA-TAPS/workflow/Snakefile \
--configfile config.yaml \
--profile /path/to/sRNA-TAPS/profile \
all_benchmark

Species-aware references: The default registry includes human, mouse, rat, zebrafish, fruit fly, c_elegans, and chicken. Human still defaults to GRCh38, but any supported species can be selected through reference.species.
If the genome FASTA or GTF do not exist at the paths in config.yaml, the pipeline derives them from reference.species and downloads the matching Ensembl release automatically. The Ensembl release is set by ensembl_release in config (default: 112). The unmasked dna.toplevel FASTA is always used — the repeat-masked version soft-masks cytosines, which would suppress genuine C→T TAPS modification signal.
If your genome files already exist on disk, all download and indexing steps are skipped. The Bowtie1 index is built once from the FASTA and reused for all samples.
Existing index: Point genome_fa, gtf, and bowtie1_index in config.yaml to your existing files. Snakemake will skip download automatically.

FastQC runs on raw FASTQs before trimming and on trimmed FASTQs after. MultiQC aggregates all results — FastQC, Trim Galore reports, and Bowtie1 alignment logs — into a single interactive HTML report at report/multiqc_report.html. For small RNA libraries, expect a dominant length peak at 18–22 nt (miRNA) and a second peak at 26–32 nt (tRNA fragments and piRNAs). All reads will contain adapter sequence since small RNA inserts are shorter than the read length.
Step 2 — Adapter Trimming
Tool: Trim Galore (Cutadapt)
Trim Galore removes the TruSeq small RNA 3′ adapter (TGGAATTCTCGGGTGCCAAGG) and quality-trims the 3′ end. Reads shorter than 18 nt or longer than 50 nt are discarded. The --small_rna flag sets sensible defaults for this library type.
Step 3 — TAPS-aware Alignment
Tool: Bowtie 1.3.1, SAMtools
Alignment is to the whole reference genome rather than a transcriptome — tRNA families (~600 gene copies), piRNA clusters, and snoRNA loci need genomic coordinates for correct downstream annotation. Four parameters are set specifically for TAPS data:
ParameterPurpose
-v 2Up to 2 total mismatches — tolerates C→T modifications without penalising them
--norcForward strand only — prevents false G→A calls on reverse strand
-k 10 --best --strataUp to 10 alignments from the best stratum; writes XA:i:N tag for fractional weighting
--samRequired for XA tag output
Step 4 — Biotype Annotation
Tool: Custom Python script (pysam), Ensembl GTF for the configured species
Reads are assigned to the highest-priority overlapping biotype using the En

Step 4 — Biotype Annotation
Tool: Custom Python script (pysam), Ensembl GTF for the configured species
Reads are assigned to the highest-priority overlapping biotype using the Ensembl GTF, and separate sorted BAMs are written per biotype per sample:
miRNA > tRNA > piRNA > snoRNA > snRNA > rRNA > lncRNA > other
A biotype composition summary (05.biotype_bams/*_biotype_summary.txt) is written alongside each BAM for downstream QC figures.
Note: TAPS enriches for rRNA relative to untreated libraries due to the pyridine borane step. Biotype proportions will differ between conditions — this is expected and not a sign of a failed experiment.
Step 5 — SNP Filtering
Tool: bcftools, custom Python
A C/T heterozygous SNP produces exactly the same signal as a TAPS m5C site. Filtering occurs in three layers before any C→T counts are made:
LayerMethodFlag
1dbSNP common C→T/G→A variants (AF ≥ 1%) — optional, set dbsnp_vcf in configSNP_KNOWN
2Cell-line-specific C→T variants called from merged no-treat BAMsSNP_SAMPLE
3No-treat C→T rate ≥ 40% (heterozygosity proxy)SNP_HET
Only positions with snp_flag == PASS proceed to statistical testing. The snp_flag column is retained in every output TSV for full traceability.

Tool: Custom Python caller (pysam, multiprocessing)

Step 7 — Background Correction
Tool: Custom Python
δ = treat_mod_rate − pb_Ctrl_mod_rate
Subtracting pb_Ctrl removes both the global pyridine borane background (~8–9%) and sequence-context-specific biases. Sites observed in only one replicate are discarded — stochastic noise is not reproducible across replicates.

Tool: bedtools intersect, Ensembl GTF for the configured species
Called sites are intersected with the Ensembl annotation to assign gene name, biotype, and feature. miRNA gene names follow miRBase nomenclature. Where a site overlaps multiple features, the most specific annotation is kept using the priority hierarchy from Step 4.

The optional benchmark suite compares sRNA-TAPS calls against three established tools: rastair (Bowtie1 BAMs, CpG-only and all-context modes), asTair (biotype-split BAMs, all contexts), and Bismark (bisulfite contrast, chemistry inverted for comparison).

Tutorial
A complete walkthrough using the 100-sample synthetic test dataset included with sRNA-TAPS. By the end you will have run the full Snakemake pipeline from raw FASTQs to called m5C sites, automatic R report figures, and, optionally, a three-tool benchmarking comparison.
Generate reproducible inputs

Launch and monitor the workflow

Verify expected signal
Check seeded miRNA sites, review report figures, and extend the run into optional benchmarking when needed.
Before you start: You need a SLURM cluster with the RNA_taps conda environment active, R packages installed (Rscript install_R_packages.R), and the sRNA-TAPS repository cloned. No pre-built genome index is required — the pipeline downloads the configured species reference automatically.

Set up the asTair environment
asTair has dependency conflicts with Snakemake and must be installed in a separate conda environment. This is a one-time setup:
# Create a dedicated Python 3.9 environment
mamba create -n astair_env -y python=3.9
# Install asTair and setuptools into it
/path/to/conda/envs/astair_env/bin/pip install astair setuptools
# Verify
/path/to/conda/envs/astair_env/bin/astair --help | head -2

# In workflow/rules/benchmark.smk, the astair_call rule shell uses:
/path/to/conda/envs/astair_env/bin/astair call \

chunks.title: Carissimi et al. (2021): human miRNA (h)m5C mapping
chunks.text: BS-miRNA-seq and MAmBA map cytosine modifications in human miRNAs. Bisulfite non-conversion does not by itself distinguish m5C from hm5C. The project curated position-resolved mature-miRNA records; use each atlas record's matching mature arm, nucleotide position and source table rather than assigning this paper to every site in a miRNA family. Antibody validation supports both modifications in mature miRNAs, not automatic chemical identification of every individual called site.

chunks.title: Konno et al. (2019): mature miRNAs in gastrointestinal cancer
chunks.text: The project's curated master records targeted MALDI-TOF-MS/MS evidence for miR-200c-3p mature C9 and miR-21-5p mature C9. These are specific miRNA/site records, not evidence that all cytosines or both arms are methylated. Interpret tissue, serum and disease observations in the study's sample context. The curated notes flag a miR-21 arm-label inconsistency in the article text; the supplementary MS/MS evidence identifies 5p.

chunks.title: Cheray et al. (2020): miRNA methylation in glioblastoma
chunks.text: The curated project records distinguish exact mature-nucleotide evidence, candidate CpG position sets from small-RNA bisulfite sequencing, and nonpositional anti-m5C immunoprecipitation array enrichment. A miRNA-level array result is not proof of a particular C position. Candidate CpG summaries from three U87 replicates must not be reported as independently measured methylation rates for every candidate nucleotide. Preserve the resolution attached to each source record.

chunks.title: Ohshiro et al. (2021): single-molecule RNA modification detection
chunks.text: Single-molecule RNA sequencing was investigated for simultaneous detection of m6A and 5mC. The project's curated master includes five exact mature-nucleotide records from this study. Consult an exact matched atlas citation before claiming a particular miRNA position; do not extrapolate a demonstrated method to all small RNAs.

chunks.title: Lü et al. (2024): purified mature-miRNA LC-MS/MS
chunks.text: Two-step hybridization purification was coupled to LC-MS/MS to measure modifications in mature miRNAs. The project's curated records classify this evidence as miRNA-level and nonpositional. Modified nucleoside abundance in purified RNA does not alone identify a modified nucleotide coordinate.

chunks.title: Zeng et al.: miRNAs in minimal change disease
chunks.text: The project's curated master includes 83 miRNA-level, nonpositional records under this publication, labeled 2026 in the local bibliography (PMID 41235950). Use the source publication for publication-date details. These records are not exact nucleotide validation and cannot establish that an arbitrary atlas C site was previously reported. This entry is a pointer to the locally curated literature, not an independently revalidated site map.

chunks.title: Haag et al. (2015): NSUN6 and tRNA C72
chunks.text: Human NSUN6 methylates C72 in specific tRNA-Cys and tRNA-Thr substrates. Recognition depends on the 3-prime CCA tail in the reported in-vitro experiments. This finding should not be generalized to every tRNA with cytosine at that coordinate. Use mature-tRNA numbering and species-specific substrate identity.

chunks.title: NSUN2-dependent methylation and tRNA fragmentation (2014)
chunks.text: Loss of NSUN2-dependent cytosine methylation increased angiogenin-mediated tRNA cleavage and accumulation of 5-prime tRNA fragments in the studied human and mouse systems, with effects on translation and cellular stress. Modification on a parental tRNA and detection in a tRNA-derived fragment are related but distinct observations. Do not infer a causal cleavage mechanism from one atlas call alone.

chunks.title: Human DNMT2 and tRNA-Asp C38 (2008)
chunks.text: Human DNMT2 catalyzes methylation of C38 in tRNA-Asp using a DNA-methyltransferase-like catalytic mechanism. DNMT2 is also known as TRDMT1. Cite substrate-specific experiments; this evidence does not assign DNMT2 as the writer for all small-RNA m5C sites.

chunks.title: NSUN3 and ALKBH1: mitochondrial tRNA-Met modification pathway (2016)
chunks.text: NSUN3 introduces m5C34 in mitochondrial tRNA-Met and ALKBH1/ABH1 oxidizes it to f5C34, expanding codon recognition. A signal at this coordinate must be interpreted with the assay's chemical specificity: pathway involvement does not prove the endpoint is unoxidized m5C. Distinguish mitochondrial tRNA-Met from cytoplasmic tRNA-Met.

chunks.title: NSUN5 and ribosomal RNA methylation (2019)
chunks.text: NSUN5 introduces m5C at human 28S rRNA C3782 and mouse 28S rRNA C3438 in the reported study. The species and reference numbering matter. A short RNA read assigned to rRNA may derive from a large rRNA precursor; do not classify the intact 28S molecule as a small RNA or transfer a coordinate between species without mapping.

chunks.title: TAPS chemistry: original DNA method (2019)
chunks.text: The original DNA TAPS method uses TET oxidation of 5mC/5hmC to 5caC and pyridine-borane reduction to dihydrouracil, producing C-to-T readout. It is a DNA study, not experimental validation of the project's RNA adaptation. Treat the sRNA-TAPS documentation as the source for its RNA workflow and controls; do not equate the two validation scopes.

chunks.title: Pyridine-borane readout and RNA oxidation products (2022)
chunks.text: Reactivity-dependent profiling of RNA 5-methylcytidine dioxygenases investigated RNA oxidation products and pyridine-borane-based readout, including mitochondrial tRNA-Met. Native oxidized cytosines can matter for interpretation of a conversion signal. Use the actual treatment and control scheme rather than labeling every C-to-T event as chemically specific m5C.
